summary: Proposes a generic architecture for Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting (AAA): a general AAA server that application-specific modules can plug into. It is experimental and sets out a design rather than a finished protocol.

eli5.summary: A building needs a guard who checks who you are, what rooms you may enter, and writes down your visit. This describes one shared guard for many different doors.

questions: how does generic aaa server work
how to do multi domain authorization
subtitle: A general framework where one AAA server handles authentication, authorization, and accounting for many applications.

tldr.problem: Different applications (LDAP, bandwidth brokers, e-commerce) each require checking who users are, what they can access, and recording their usage, but building separate AAA systems for each is inefficient.
tldr.mechanism: A generic AAA server contains a rule-based engine and interfaces with application-specific modules (ASMs). The server handles standard AAA logic and forwards requests between domains; the ASMs handle application-specific details.
tldr.outcome: Organizations can deploy one AAA infrastructure serving multiple applications. Requests combine constraints from different systems (e.g., dial-in access permission plus available bandwidth plus account credit) in a single transaction.

today: RFC 2903 is Experimental and not obsoleted. It remains an influential architecture document in AAA development. Later standards like RADIUS and DIAMETER built on related concepts. However, a universally deployed 'generic AAA server' standard never fully materialized, and different applications continue to implement or modify AAA protocols for their specific needs.

sections.title: The AAA Problem Across Domains
sections.content:
This RFC proposes a generic AAA architecture—a framework for Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting that can serve many applications. It builds on earlier work in the IETF's AAA Working Group, focusing on a layered protocol model and a central generic server that delegates application-specific work to modular components.

The challenge is that authentication, authorization, and accounting requirements vary by application. A user dialing in requires network access control. A bandwidth broker requires QoS reservation. An e-commerce service requires payment verification. Rather than deploy separate AAA systems for each, the RFC proposes one generic AAA server containing a rule-based engine, communicating with Application Specific Modules (ASMs) that understand each application's unique needs.
sections.eli5: Instead of a factory having separate security for the front door, the cafeteria, the computer room, and the warehouse, hire one head of security. She applies general rules ('Show your ID,' 'You must be trained for the chemical room') but defers to specialists ('The chef decides who goes in the kitchen').

sections.title: Components of the Generic Server
sections.content:
The generic AAA server contains five key architectural components. The authorization rule evaluation engine is the logic core: it receives a request, inspects it, and determines what decision to make. The Application Specific Module (ASM) is a separate component that handles application-specific knowledge—a bandwidth broker ASM understands QoS, while a payment ASM understands accounts and credit.

An authorization event log stores time-stamped records of all authorizations granted, for auditing and as input to future decisions (e.g., 'deny access if the same user already has 10 active sessions'). A policy repository stores the rules and the catalog of available services. Finally, request forwarding allows AAA servers in different domains to query each other, enabling complex authorization decisions that span organizations.
sections.eli5: The security office has a filing cabinet (the policy repository), a log book (event log), a rulebook (the engine), specialists (ASMs), and phones to call other security offices (request forwarding).

sections.title: Multi-Domain Authorization
sections.content:
The RFC emphasizes multi-domain architecture: AAA servers in different organizations need to cooperate. A request might combine authorizations from multiple sources. For example, a remote experiment request might need approval from a dial-in provider (network access), a bandwidth broker (QoS reservation), and an accounting system (funds available)—potentially run by three different organizations.

Each organization's AAA server uses a peer-to-peer protocol to communicate with others. The generic server forwards the components of a request to the appropriate remote servers, collects the responses, and assembles a final authorization decision. This requires a common naming space across domains and the ability to route requests correctly. Legacy AAA protocols like RADIUS can be encapsulated within the new protocol, protecting existing investments while enabling new functionality.
sections.eli5: You want to fly a drone from home via a rental service. The rental service checks: Does your internet provider allow it (dial-in)? Is the airspace available (bandwidth)? Do you have enough money (account)? All three organizations' AAA servers talk to each other and together say yes or no.

sections.title: Layering the AAA Functions
sections.content:
The RFC proposes a layered protocol model with distinct service layers: Application Specific Service Layer (handles application details), Presentation Service Layer (formats data), Transaction/Session Management Service Layer (manages state and sequences), and Reliable/Secure Transport Service Layer (transport and encryption).

Each layer has its own protocol, optimized for its specific role. This design allows substituting one protocol for another at a given layer without disrupting the rest (e.g., replacing RADIUS with a different hop-by-hop protocol, or using CORBA/CDR for the presentation layer). It also allows vendors to support different layers, and enables legacy protocols to be encapsulated within the new framework. The RFC notes that this section is exploratory, not a finished reference model, as the interface between generic server and ASMs may be more complex than simple layering captures.
sections.eli5: Think of a multi-level approval process: bottom layer is secure delivery (locked envelope), next layer is routing (where does the request go), next is meaning (what does this request mean), top is application-specific rules (should we approve this?).

sections.title: Design Principles and Future Work
sections.content:
The RFC identifies key design principles: the generic server must be application-agnostic, knowing nothing about application-specific data except how to forward it opaque. A standard AAA protocol must support multiple services and applications in a single request. The protocol should be peer-to-peer, not enforcing client/server roles. Naming becomes critical: servers must agree on how to name services, resources, rules, and other entities across domains.

The RFC also identifies areas needing further work: discovering what authorizations a server can grant, determining what a request must contain for a specific authorization, and managing rules across multiple domains. In a multi-domain environment with contracts between organizations, rules must be created and maintained automatically. The long-term goal is a 'future-proof' protocol: unforeseen requirements can be encoded as application-specific information and referenced in rules, without changing the core protocol.
sections.eli5: Key challenge: make the system so flexible that when a new type of request shows up next year, you don't have to reprogram everything—just add a new rule to the policy book.
